summary.summary: West Berkshire's draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 is dominated by financial sustainability, described as 'extremely difficult' and corroborated by a CIPFA Financial Resilience review, external auditor KPMG, and the s151 Officer's own section 25 statement. The provisional 2025/26 outturn was £192.9m net expenditure against a £183.4m net budget; the council has again secured Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), which it stresses is short-term, must be repaid with compound interest, and is not a sustainable solution. The EFS requirement for 2025/26 has been reduced from £20m to £17m as the Finance Improvement Plan starts to bite (outturn improved £3.2m between Q3 and Q4; the DSG high-needs deficit improved £4.8m against forecast). Most striking for a lender: the AGS explicitly names a section 114 scenario as the risk if the DSG statutory override (in place to 31 March 2028) ends before the High Needs Stability Grant write-off of roughly 90% of the deficit materialises.

signals.headline: Exceptional Financial Support secured again for a second year to protect the General Fund; the £17m EFS requirement for 2025/26 is reduced from an earlier £20m estimate, but EFS 'must be repaid with compound interest' and is explicitly not a sustainable long-term solution (page 3-4)
signals.why: Continuing reliance on repayable exceptional support, even at a reduced level, means the underlying structural income/expenditure gap has not yet closed.

signals.headline: AGS states directly that if the DSG statutory override (protecting the balance sheet until 31 March 2028) ends before the High Needs Stability Grant write-off of circa 90% of the deficit lands, the council is exposed to 'catastrophic balance-sheet failure, resulting in a s114 scenario' (page 6)
signals.why: This is the council naming its own route to insolvency notice in a formal governance document, not an external commentator's inference.

signals.headline: High Needs (DSG) block deficit improved £4.8m against forecast outturn in-year, but remains kept off the general fund only by the statutory override to 31 March 2028; securing High Needs Stability Grant funding to write off circa 90% of it is the top-listed governance action for 2026/27-Feb 2027 (pages 4-6)
signals.why: The deficit is shrinking but the balance-sheet protection is time-limited and the write-off is not yet secured.

compliance.notes: Technically strong on the core prudential-indicator, liability-benchmark, MRP and affordability disclosures: full CFR reconciliation, liability benchmark charted over the full debt maturity profile and used as a live tool, detailed asset-life MRP policy, and a frank EFS-driven affordability/distress narrative (financing ratio breaching the 10% rule from 27/28). Weakest areas: no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02, core) despite repeatedly warning the Council is becoming 'fully exposed to interest rate risk'; commercial-investment proportionality asserted but not quantified (COM-03, core); and a cluster of absent items - no quantitative investment risk indicator (INV-06), no IMPs (COM-05), no guarantees/contingent-liability review (RISK-05), no derivatives policy (RISK-06), no ESG policy (ESG-01), no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05) and no third-party/pension monies attribution (GOV-07).

gaps.evidence: TMSS §5.4d states the net-income-to-net-revenue-stream indicator 'is required'; Appendix C p.26-27 discloses commercial-property net income (£2.88m 24/25) and rates of return
TMSS §5.4 sets out the Prudential Code para 51-53 requirements on service/commercial investment and the Council's compliant position
TMSS §5.2c/§5.4a state the proportionality principle (plausible losses absorbed in budgets/reserves); Appendix C discloses the £39.9m debt-financed commercial property portfolio
TMSS §5.5d states limits on total service and commercial investment are required
TMSS §9.5-9.6 references that the counterparty limits relate to both specified and non-specified investments

findings.headline: Pothole and road edge repairs completed within 28-day target improved to 93.3%, up from 88.9% in the prior quarter and now tracking toward the 95% target by Q2.
findings.detail: This measure was Red for all of 2025-26 (ranging 76.8%-89.2%) and is now Amber with clear upward trajectory. Council is working closely with contractor to identify and rectify shortcomings. Clear operational improvement trend in a core highway maintenance service.
findings.matters: Highway maintenance is core asset management. Sustained underperformance can spiral defect damage, create liability exposure, and damage reputation. The improving trend demonstrates the council can fix operational performance problems through contractor engagement.
findings.figures: 93.3% (Q1 26-27) vs 95% target; up from 88.9% (Q4 25-26); Red throughout 2025-26 range 76.8%-89.2%.
findings.quote: This is a clear improvement from 2025/26 Q4 and on full year figures for 2025/26.

findings.headline: Household waste recycling rate fell to 52.7%, below the 57% target and down from 54.5% in the previous quarter.
findings.detail: Decline attributed to contractor sending wood waste for recovery rather than recycling due to weak recycled material markets. Extreme heat in June reduced garden waste tonnages. Contractor's year-end forecast 55.7%, still below target. Q1 data provisional and subject to DEFRA validation.
findings.matters: Recycling rate is both an environmental performance metric and a potential contractual/cost issue. Declines can trigger contract performance queries and suggest external market and weather pressures on waste contractor performance.
findings.figures: 52.7% (Q1) vs 57% target; down from 54.5% (Q4 25-26); contractor forecast 55.7% year-end.
findings.quote: Wider industry challenges have meant our contractor has had to send wood for recovery and not recycling which has led to a fall in recycling rate, however, they are hoping that the market for recycled wood will pick up from July onwards.

findings.headline: Staff turnover remained at 15.0% against target of 13%, with the council stating the figure 'is likely to remain higher than the target given the continued restructure proposals the council continues to undertake.'
findings.detail: Turnover consistently above target throughout the year. Top three reasons for resignation: career development, relocation, health reasons. Vacancy rate 15.5% (down from 17.9%). Council signals structural nature of problem: ongoing reorganisations will sustain elevated turnover. This creates dual pressure—ongoing recruitment costs and sustained service delivery disruption.
findings.matters: Persistent above-target staff turnover indicates difficulty retaining staff, creating direct costs (recruitment, training, lost knowledge) and indirect costs (service disruption, quality degradation). Council's own statement that restructures will keep turnover elevated signals loss of institutional capacity.
findings.figures: 15.0% outturn vs 13% target (Q1); 15.5% vacancy rate vs 17.9% previous quarter; consistently above target throughout year.
findings.quote: However, it is likely that the figure will remain higher than the target given the continued restructure proposals the council continues to undertake.

findings.headline: Rough sleeping increased to 13 people on a single night (target 6) and long-term entrenched homelessness rose to 10 (target 3), with affordable housing completions at 24 against target of 37.
findings.detail: Both rough-sleeping measures are new for 2026-27. Council attributes increase partly to warmer months but notes 'those who are entrenched in homelessness has increased.' Housing completion pipeline delayed, with registered provider completions typically Q4 due to construction practices. Housing shortage is stated reason for failure to meet relief duty (50.9% secured 6+ months accommodation vs 55% target) and is driving the rough-sleeper cohort.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness and entrenched rough sleeping indicate unmet housing need and growing demand on council services requiring sustained expenditure. Housing shortage constrains the council's ability to discharge statutory homelessness relief duty, increasing pressure on temporary accommodation services.
findings.figures: 13 rough sleepers vs target 6; 10 long-term rough sleepers vs target 3; 24 affordable homes completed vs 37 target; 50.9% relief duty success vs 55% target.
findings.quote: Those who are entrenched in homelessness has increased.

findings.headline: Safeguarding outcomes in adult protection declined, with only 56.3% of Section 42 enquiries resulting in fully achieved outcomes, compared to 68% target.
findings.detail: Outcomes have deteriorated consistently through year (68%→61.7%→63.5%→62.7%→56.3%). Of 142 Q1 cases, only 80 achieved full outcomes, 48 achieved partial outcomes, 14 achieved none. Council has commissioned audit of unachieved cases. Trend is downward despite council noting partially achieved cases increased.
findings.matters: Declining safeguarding outcomes indicate adult protection service is under capacity or strain, creating governance risk, regulatory exposure, and reputational damage. Councils have non-discretionary duty to protect vulnerable adults.
findings.figures: 56.3% vs 68% target (Q1); 80/142 full outcomes; YTD deterioration from 68% to 56.3%.
findings.quote: Although % fully achieved has dropped, partially achieved has increased. Only 14 out of 142 cases where outcomes not achieved.
